chunks: Which layers should be ground. The question: Which layer(s) should be the ground layer(s)?
Ground layers go right next to the signal layers, so every signal has a solid path home directly beneath it.
On a 4-layer board that means ground on layer 2, just under the top signals. On a 6-layer board it means ground on layers 2 and 5.
The goal is a small loop between the signal and its return current.
Think of a road with a return lane. Every car that drives out must come back. If the return lane runs right alongside, the round trip is short and tidy.
If the only way back is a distant highway, each trip is long and traffic spills everywhere. Current works the same way.
At high frequency it comes back through the plane directly under the trace, and a close plane keeps the loop small. A gap in the plane acts like a closed road, forcing a detour.
The same trace with the plane close (left) and far (right). With the plane close, the return current is confined near the trace.
With the plane far away, the return current spreads wide, so neighbouring traces share the same return region and couple.
Return current: the current that flows back to the source to complete the loop ("Ground plane pros and cons"). Loop area: the area enclosed by the signal and its return path.
Smaller means less radiation and crosstalk. Inductance: how strongly a loop resists changes in current, in nanohenries (nH). It grows with loop size.
Reactance: the opposition, in ohms, that an inductance gives to a changing current. It rises with frequency.
Plane split or slot: a gap in a plane that forces the return current to detour ("When and why to separate grounds").
Take a 0. 3 mm trace, using the page's approximation. With ground 0. 2 mm below, the loop inductance is about 0. 32 nanohenries per mm. With ground 1.
6 mm below, as on a 2-layer board, it is about 0. 73 nanohenries per mm. Over 50 mm that is 16 nanohenries against 36 nanohenries.
At 100 megahertz these give reactances of about 10 ohms and 23 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"Ground goes directly next to the signal layers: layer 2 on a four-layer board, layers 2 and 5 on a six-layer.
High-frequency return current flows in the plane right under the trace, so a close, solid ground gives a small loop, less radiation and crosstalk, and predictable impedance.
A ground plane between two signal layers also shields them. The plane has to be continuous, so I don't cut it with slots or route across gaps."
